datasets.title: Bankruptcy filings by chapter, court district, state and county, quarterly (U.S. Courts)
datasets.summary: Bankruptcy cases commenced in the 12 months ending on each quarter-end, from the U.S. Courts' Tables F-5A (by county and chapter), F-2 (by court district, chapter and business or nonbusiness debt) and F (cases filed, terminated and pending). One record per area: the United States, every state, DC and territory, 93 court districts and about 3,100 counties. Each gives the latest period's cases by Chapter 7, 11, 13 and other chapters, the business and nonbusiness split, the change on the year before, filings per 1,000 residents (Census 2025 population estimates) and the court's figures for the six earlier periods. Every table is checked against the court's own totals row. Counts of cases, not outcomes: a filing is not a discharge.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where debt trouble reaches the federal bankruptcy courts, how Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 mix in a state or county, and which districts are growing, before you size a bankruptcy practice's market. It counts cases commenced, not people helped or fees earned.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Bankruptcy filings by chapter, court district, state and county, quarterly (U.S. Courts), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23739952, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.title: The new-lawyer pipeline by jurisdiction: bar exam pass rates and new admissions, 2025
datasets.summary: For every US jurisdiction that reports to the National Conference of Bar Examiners (the 50 states, DC, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Palau, Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands): the overall 2025 bar exam pass rate, how many new lawyers were admitted in 2025 (by examination, by transferred UBE score and on motion), how admissions by exam or transferred score changed since 2021, and how much of the total came from transferred scores and from motion. NCBE reserves its published tables, so this dataset republishes none of them: every figure is one we derive from them (a rate, a sum, a change, a share), credited to NCBE with a link to the table it comes from. Each jurisdiction's rows add up to NCBE's own totals row before anything is published.
datasets.uses: Use it to size the new-lawyer market in a state: how many people are licensed each year, how many arrive by passing the exam, by moving a score or by moving their license, and whether that supply is growing. A state with a falling count and a low pass rate is losing new lawyers to its neighbours. Read it beside the lawyer wages and law-offices datasets before you decide where to recruit or advertise to new lawyers.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, The new-lawyer pipeline by jurisdiction: bar exam pass rates and new admissions, 2025, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23721443, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.title: Probative benchmarks, 2025–2026
datasets.summary: Probative benchmarks, 2025–2026: aggregated, rounded, and small groups suppressed. Our data on law-firm marketing, shown as bands, named tiers and rounded values, one table per file. The public tables cover how quickly inquiries become signed clients, phone calls and signed clients, AI answers and organic search clicks, search-ad click costs, what people type, calls from ads, Local Services Ads leads, inquiries by quarter and ad cost per signed client. Each row gives the measure, the band or tier, its unit and a rough size band. Every value is aggregated across many observations; values resting on too few observations, or resting mostly on a few, are suppressed for privacy. Values are approximate, so read the band, not a point. The methods page defines every measure and the protection steps.
datasets.uses: Use it to compare your own firm's figure with a band, not to predict a result: a band is a range and a tier is a named range, so a firm above or below it is a prompt to look closer, not proof of a problem.

datasets.title: California court filings by county: civil, criminal, family, juvenile, probate and appeals, fiscal years 2023–24 and 2024–25
datasets.summary: How many cases were filed in each of California's 58 superior courts (one per county) and statewide, by case type, from the Judicial Council of California's Court Statistics Reports: unlimited civil (motor-vehicle injury, other injury and wrongful death, other civil), limited civil, unlawful detainer, small claims, felonies and misdemeanors, family law, juvenile, probate, mental health and appeals. One record per county and case type, with the prior year beside it. In every table the 58 counties add up exactly to the report's own statewide row, and the totals inside each row add up too. Counts only: no lawyer or firm is listed or ranked.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where the legal work is. A filing is a new case opened in the county's superior court, so the counts show how much demand each practice area has in each county; they do not show how many of those people hired a lawyer. Filings are for a state fiscal year (July 1 to June 30). Compare a county's count with the statewide row and with the year before, and read the report's own limits before you rely on a small county's figure.

datasets.title: Federal civil filings by nature of suit and district, 12-month periods since 2018
datasets.summary: How many civil cases were filed in each of the 94 U.S. district courts and nationwide, by nature of suit, from the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts' Statistical Tables for the Federal Judiciary: Table C-3 (the 94 districts by case type: contract, real property, torts, civil rights, prisoner petitions, labor, Social Security, intellectual property and more, U.S. cases and private cases) and Table C-2 (the nation by about 100 natures of suit, such as product liability, medical malpractice, employment, the Fair Labor Standards Act, ERISA and consumer credit, with the basis of jurisdiction). One record per district and case type for the latest 12 months, with the year before and the history of every earlier table, and one record per nature of suit nationwide. In every table the 94 districts add up exactly to the national Total row, every circuit adds up to its districts and every nature-of-suit group adds up to the rows under it. Counts only: no lawyer or firm is listed or ranked.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where federal civil cases are filed and which kinds are growing. A filing is a civil case commenced in a district court in the 12-month period, so the counts show how much federal demand each case type has in each district; they do not show how many of those people hired a lawyer, and they leave out state courts. Prisoner petitions are kept apart from the injury, employment and consumer groups. Compare a district's count with the nation and with the year before, and read the flag on small counts before you rely on a percent change.

datasets.title: CFPB complaints about debt collection, credit reporting and debt management, by state and month
datasets.summary: Complaints that consumers filed with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) about debt collection, credit reporting and credit repair, and debt or credit management, counted by state, month, product and issue from January 2018, with the last 12 months set against the 12 before and per 100,000 residents. One record per state, DC, Puerto Rico and territory for each of the three product groups, with the share of complaints the company answered on time and the issue people raised most. The counts come from the CFPB's own Consumer Complaint Database search API, as aggregates, so no complaint, narrative, company name or ZIP code is ever copied; for every month the issue counts add up to the bureau's own count for each product group. Small counts are suppressed by the EEOC, and a state with its own fair-employment agency sends part of its charges there.

datasets.title: Fatal crashes by county and type: trucks, motorcycles, pedestrians and bicyclists, NHTSA FARS 2019 to 2024
datasets.summary: Fatal motor-vehicle crashes in every US county, state and the nation for 2019 to 2024, from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS). One record per county, state and the US: fatal crashes and deaths in the newest year, the crashes that involved a large truck, a motorcycle, a pedestrian or a bicyclist, the pedestrians, bicyclists and motorcyclists killed, alcohol-impaired, speeding and work-zone crashes, rural and urban roads, deaths per 100,000 residents, and every earlier year. Every county-year equals the accident table's own rows, and the counties add up to the state and the state to the nation. 2019 to 2023 are NHTSA's final files; 2024 is its first (annual report) release. The county-by-year table is at /research/fatal-crashes-by-county/data.csv. Counts only.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where fatal crashes concentrate, which counties have the most large-truck, motorcycle, pedestrian or bicyclist deaths, and how rural and urban counties compare per 100,000 residents. Look up a county by its 5-digit FIPS code. It counts crashes, not injuries or claims, and says nothing about fault.

datasets.title: Law firm size, solos and receipts, by state: Census SUSB 2022, Nonemployer Statistics 2024 and Economic Census 2022
datasets.summary: How big U.S. law firms are and what they take in, for the US, every state and DC, from three Census Bureau sources. Employer law firms (NAICS 541110, offices of lawyers) by number of employees (fewer than 5, 5 to 9, 10 to 19, 20 to 99, 100 to 499, 500 or more) with their employees, payroll and receipts, from the Statistics of U.S. Businesses (SUSB) 2022. Businesses with no employees (mostly sole practitioners) and their receipts, by legal form, from Nonemployer Statistics 2024, which publishes legal services (NAICS 5411) as one group. Firm counts, receipts, the share of receipts held by the largest firms and firms by receipts size from the Economic Census 2022. One record per jurisdiction and class. Every size-class row adds up to its total row; classes the Census Bureau does not publish are left empty and flagged, never estimated.
datasets.uses: Use it to see how many law firms in a state are small, how much they take in, and how many solo practitioners sit outside the employer counts, before you plan marketing for a solo or small firm. Look up your state: the records give each size class with its share of firms and of receipts, the solo (nonemployer) count and receipts per solo, and the Economic Census cross-check. The sources cover different years (2022, 2024, 2022), and a firm with offices in several states is counted in each, so compare shares within a state or the US, not state counts added together.

datasets.title: Legal need by county: who may need a lawyer, from the American Community Survey
datasets.summary: The people in every U.S. county who may need a lawyer, counted from the Census Bureau's American Community Survey 2020 to 2024 5-year estimates: residents aged 65 and over, residents who are not U.S. citizens, foreign-born residents who arrived since 2010, residents who speak English less than very well (and Spanish speakers among them), divorced residents (and, for states, people divorced in the last year), veterans and veterans with a VA disability rating, residents with a disability, households on SSI, renter households and renters paying 30 or 50 percent of income on rent, residents without health insurance, workers who drive to work and median household income. One record per county (3,144, in the 50 states and DC), per state and for the US, each measure with its 90% margin of error and its share of the population it is counted in.
datasets.uses: Use it as the denominator of a local market: how many people in a county could need an immigration, family, elder-law, estate-planning, veterans' disability, Social Security disability, landlord-tenant or injury lawyer, and how that compares with the state. Pair it with the law-offices, deserts, fatal-crashes or immigration-courts datasets by county FIPS code. Agents can look up a state's counties, compare states, or search a county by name and measure.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Legal need by county: who may need a lawyer, from the American Community Survey, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23741886, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). Legal need by county: who may need a lawyer, from the American Community Survey (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23741886
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are survey estimates of people with a characteristic, not counts of legal problems or cases: a renter, a veteran or a noncitizen does not necessarily need a lawyer. Each estimate has a margin of error, and small counties' estimates are rough.

datasets.title: Legal-services prices and jobs, monthly (BLS CPI, PPI and CES)
datasets.summary: Month by month since 2017, what consumers pay for legal services (Consumer Price Index), what law offices receive for their work (Producer Price Index for offices of lawyers, overall and by type of work where BLS publishes it), and how many people work in legal services (Current Employment Statistics), each next to the all-items or services index where that helps. Every value is read from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' own database with its series id, base period, and a preliminary flag while BLS may still revise it. The consumer index measures a basket item, not a law firm's billing rate. Counts and index values only.
datasets.uses: Use it to put a fee, a billing rate or a hiring plan against the official price record. Look up the consumer legal-services index, the producer price index for offices of lawyers, or legal-services employment; each series comes with its last 24 months and the year-over-year change. To adjust a fee from an earlier year to today's prices, use the legal inflation calculator. To test a fee you set years ago, read the consumer legal-services index for the month you set it and for the latest month: the ratio shows how far legal prices moved in between, and the producer series for law offices shows whether firms' billings moved faster or slower than what clients paid.

datasets.title: Statutes of limitations by state: personal injury, medical malpractice, wrongful death, product liability and property damage
datasets.summary: The filing deadline the statute sets for five kinds of civil claims in every US state and DC: personal injury, medical malpractice, wrongful death, product liability and property damage. Each record gives the period in the statute's own words, the citation, a link to the state's official code site, a verbatim quote, and the date read; where the same text says so, it adds whether the period runs from discovery and any outer limit (statute of repose). Cells we could not read in the official text are marked U and left blank. No calculator and no deadline arithmetic: tolling and exceptions apply.
datasets.uses: Look up one state and claim type, then read the quoted statute and its exceptions before relying on it. For marketing pages and intake scripts that mention filing deadlines, cite the statute and link the official text, never a bare number.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Statutes of limitations by state: personal injury, medical malpractice, wrongful death, product liability and property damage, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23721436, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are the periods as each statute states them, read in the official code on the date shown. Tolling, discovery rules, notice-of-claim deadlines for claims against a government, minors' rules and other exceptions can shorten or lengthen the time to file, and statutes change. Check the statute and ask a lawyer licensed in the state before relying on a deadline.

datasets.title: Mass-tort docket tracker, federal MDL pending actions by month since 2019
datasets.summary: Pending actions in every federal multidistrict litigation (MDL), from the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation's monthly 'Pending MDL Dockets by Actions Pending' reports. One record per docket: the court's docket title, the transferee district, the docket type, actions now pending, actions ever filed, the change over 12 months, the peak pending count, and the docket's monthly pending count since 2019. Version 1.1 adds the 14 MDLs the court closed between 2026-01-01 and 2026-10-01 (dateClosed set, the peak and last count from the monthly series) and the court's reports by district and by docket type, with monthly groupings of the series. Every report's rows add up exactly to the court's own totals row. The full monthly series, judge included, is at /data/v1/mdl/history/index.json (one CSV per year); the district, type and closed-MDL files are at /data/v1/mdl/reports/index.json. Counts and dates only.

datasets.measurementTechnique: Each monthly report of the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation (“Distribution of Pending MDL Dockets by Actions Pending”) is fetched from jpml.uscourts.gov and parsed by machine. datasets.title: Legal-marketing ethics opinions, 2004–2026
datasets.summary: An index of US state and ABA ethics opinions, committee guidelines and court rulings on lawyer advertising and marketing, from 2004 to 2026 (most from 2015 on, plus earlier landmarks): lead generators, pay-per-lead, reviews, testimonials, trade names, websites, social media, chatbots and AI tools, competitor keywords and more. Version 1.1 adds an AI sub-index: 14 AI opinions coded on six marketing questions (chatbot disclosure, AI-made ads, intake and solicitation, superiority claims, confidentiality in marketing tools, and fees). Each record gives the issuing body, number, date, topics, a one-sentence holding in our words, a practical step, whether it is still in force, the official link, an exact short quote and the date read. It is not the opinions' full text.
datasets.uses: Use it before you try a new kind of marketing. If you want to buy leads, pay a referral platform, quote a client review, run a chatbot or bid on a rival firm's name, search the index for that topic and your state first. You will see which committees have already answered the question, what they said in plain words, what step it points to, and whether the answer still stands. Then read the opinion itself through its official link before you rely on it. Typical questions it answers: can a firm pay a lead generator per lead or per signed case; may an ad quote a client's online review; may a firm buy a competitor's name as a search keyword; who is responsible when a chatbot on the firm's site answers a legal question; and whether a trade name or a website domain can imply a specialty. Each answer names the committee or court, the opinion number and its date, so a partner can hand the citation straight to counsel. Version 1.1 also answers a newer question: what has each bar said about AI in marketing? Filter to the topic "ai" to see the 14 AI opinions, and read the six coded fields to see which ones say anything about chatbots, AI-made ads, intake, superiority claims, confidentiality and fees.

datasets.summary: How many cases are added to Texas trial-court dockets, by county, court level and case group, from the Office of Court Administration's annual statistical reports: district courts (civil, family, juvenile, criminal), constitutional county courts (civil, criminal, juvenile) and statutory county courts (civil, family, juvenile, felony, misdemeanor), for Texas fiscal years 2024 and 2025 (September 1 to August 31). Each record gives the cases added, the year before, the cases disposed and the cases pending at year end, and a rate per 100,000 residents for county rows. In every table the counties add up exactly to the report's own statewide row, and the district-court rows reconcile to the separate Activity Detail workbook. Counts only: no lawyer or firm is listed or ranked. The schema carries a state code so other states' machine-readable caseloads can be added under the same keys; case types are compared only within a state.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where the legal work is in Texas. A case added is a new case or motion put on a court's docket, so the counts show how much demand each practice area has in each county; they do not show how many of those people hired a lawyer. Compare a county with the statewide row, with the year before, and per 100,000 residents. Read the court level: the same county can have district-court cases and county-court cases, and one level's count is not the county's total. Case types are the state's own categories and are not comparable across states.

datasets.title: VA-accredited attorneys and claims agents per veteran, by state, with county counts and Board of Veterans' Appeals outcomes by type of representation
datasets.summary: How many attorneys and claims agents the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs has accredited to help with benefit claims, counted by the state (and, in the county file, the county) of each person's business address, against the VA's own projection of living veterans (VetPop2023, rounded to the nearest 1,000). One record per state, DC, Puerto Rico and territory, one for the United States and one for people whose list entry shows no US state, each with attorneys, claims agents, veterans per accredited attorney, accredited attorneys and agents per 100,000 veterans, the number accredited in the last 12 months and how many counties have none. Records for the Board of Veterans' Appeals add its decisions in fiscal year 2024 by outcome and by type of representative. The VA's lists name every person; only counts are read, and no name, phone number, registration number or ZIP code is published.
datasets.uses: Use it to see where VA-accredited attorneys and agents have offices compared with the veterans a state is projected to have, which counties have none, and how many were accredited recently, before you plan veterans' benefits marketing. Look up your state: the record gives the counts, the ratios and the history since this dataset began. The count is by business address, so it shows where offices are, not how many veterans each person serves, and the veteran counts are a projection.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, VA-accredited attorneys and claims agents per veteran, by state, with county counts and Board of Veterans' Appeals outcomes by type of representation, version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23740008, licensed CC BY 4.0.
datasets.citation: Probative. (2026). VA-accredited attorneys and claims agents per veteran, by state, with county counts and Board of Veterans' Appeals outcomes by type of representation (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23740008
datasets.disclaimer: Not legal advice. These are counts of people on the VA's public accreditation lists and of Board of Veterans' Appeals decisions, kept for marketing planning. An accreditation is the VA's permission to help with claims, not an endorsement or a measure of quality, and the counts say nothing about any veteran's claim. Deadlines and fees are for your own counsel.

datasets.mcpLine: VA-accredited attorneys and claims agents per veteran by state, county counts, and appeals outcomes by representation.
datasets.measurementTechnique: The VA Office of General Counsel's two complete lists (attorneys and claims agents) are downloaded with the same single form POST the page's Download button sends, parsed in memory and counted by the state in each business address, by county (the ZIP code's county in the Census ZCTA-to-county file) and by year accredited, then discarded; no name, phone, registration number or ZIP code is stored. Counts must add up to the lists' row counts, county counts to each state, and three states are matched against the VA's own search form. Veterans are VetPop2023 county rows (which add up to its state table) at the latest September 30, rounded to the nearest 1,000. The Board's table rows must add up to its grand total and its decision count.

datasets.title: Workplace injuries and fatal work injuries by state and industry (BLS SOII and CFOI)
datasets.summary: How often workers are hurt on the job in each state and industry, and how many die: the nonfatal injury and illness rate per 100 full-time workers for private-industry sectors and detailed industries in the states BLS publishes (Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses, 2024), and the number and rate of fatal work injuries in every state and DC, with the major cause and the industry rate (Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries, 2024). Every record carries its BLS series or table. Survey estimates carry a relative standard error and a noise flag; figures BLS does not publish are marked suppressed and never filled in. It is statistics about industries and states, never about a named employer.
datasets.uses: Use it to see which industries hurt workers most in a state, how a state's injury rate and fatal-injury rate compare with the nation, and what causes the deaths. Look up a state: each record gives the rate, the count, how precise the estimate is and the year-by-year trend where BLS publishes one. These are rates for whole industries, not for any one workplace, so they do not say whether a particular injury is covered by workers' compensation.
datasets.attribution: Source: Probative, Workplace injuries and fatal work injuries by state and industry (BLS SOII and CFOI), version 1.0.0, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23740010, licensed CC BY 4.0.

datasets.mcpLine: Workplace injuries and fatal work injuries by state and industry, from BLS SOII and CFOI: rates, case counts and the riskiest sectors.
datasets.measurementTechnique: Nonfatal rates and case counts are read from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses (SOII) time series IS by series id: total recordable cases, private industry, by state and industry, with the relative standard error. Fatal injury counts, causes and rates are read from the Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries (CFOI) state tables. Cells BLS does not publish are recorded as suppressed with no value. Nothing is imputed and no employer is named.
